title: What's this?
goal: Face the thing that makes most beginners give up: every German noun has a gender, and that gender has to be learned along with the word.
bekal: ask what something is called (*Was ist das?*)
guess a noun's gender from its ending

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Im Klassenzimmer
dialogs.intro: Marek has just moved up from the beginners' class. He knows lots of words, but always trips over the little word in front of them.

lines.speaker: Frau Weber:
lines.text: Das ist ein Wörterbuch. Das Wörterbuch ist neu.
lines.id: That's a dictionary. The dictionary is new.
lines.literal: that is a dictionary. the dictionary is new.

lines.speaker: Marek:
lines.text: Und das hier? Ist das ein Heft?
lines.id: And this one? Is this a notebook?
lines.literal: and that here? is that a notebook?

lines.speaker: Frau Weber:
lines.text: Nein, das ist kein Heft. Das ist eine Zeitung.
lines.id: No, that's not a notebook. That's a newspaper.
lines.literal: no, that is no notebook. that is a newspaper.

lines.speaker: Marek:
lines.text: Ach so. Die Zeitung ist sehr interessant.
lines.id: Oh, I see. The newspaper is very interesting.
lines.literal: ah so. the newspaper is very interesting.

lines.speaker: Frau Weber:
lines.text: Genau, der Stuhl. Und die Tafel ist dort.
lines.id: Exactly, the chair. And the board is over there.
lines.literal: exactly, the chair. and the board is there.

lines.speaker: Frau Weber:
lines.text: Ja, das sind Fenster. Und das sind die Türen.
lines.id: Yes, those are windows. And those are the doors.
lines.literal: yes, that are windows. and that are the doors.

lines.speaker: Marek:
lines.text: Das ist schwer! Der, die, das — warum?
lines.id: This is hard! Der, die, das — why?
lines.literal: that is heavy! der, die, das — why?

lines.speaker: Frau Weber:
lines.text: Keine Angst. Lernen Sie das Wort und den Artikel zusammen, immer.
lines.id: Don't worry. Learn the word and the article together, always.
lines.literal: no fear. learn you the word and the article together, always.

notes: ***Das ist…* is always *das*, whatever it points to.** Look at line 2: *Das ist **ein** Wörterbuch*, then ***Das** Wörterbuch ist neu*. The first *das* means "this/that" and never changes; the second *das* is the article belonging to *Wörterbuch*. Two words that look the same, two different jobs.
**For plural things, *das ist* becomes *das sind*.** *Das sind Fenster* — "those are windows". What changes is the verb, not the *das*.
***ein* and *eine* have no plural.** *ein Stuhl* → *Stühle* (no article at all), just as English drops *a* in the plural: *a chair* → *chairs*.

***kein* = *nicht* + *ein*.** To negate a noun, don't use *nicht*: *Das ist **kein** Heft*, not *das ist nicht ein Heft*. Its form follows the noun's gender, just like *ein* — and unlike *ein*, *kein* **does** have a plural: *keine Bücher*.
***auf Deutsch*** = "in German". *Wie heißt das auf Deutsch?* will be the sentence you use most in your first year; learn it whole.

***Genau*** ("exactly") is the word you'll hear most in everyday German conversation — for confirming, agreeing, or just filling a pause. Its neighbors: *ach so* ("oh, I see") and *alles klar* ("all right, got it").

grammars.title: der, die, das — and how to guess them
body: German has three noun genders, and each has a pair of articles: one for a thing already known (*der/die/das*, like "the"), and one for a thing just mentioned (*ein/eine*, like "a").
after: The last row carries a piece of good news textbooks rarely mention: **every plural noun takes *die***, no exceptions, whatever the gender of the singular. One rule that is truly exception-free.
About 80% of nouns can be guessed from their ending. The list below doesn't cover everything, but it covers the most common ones:

grammars.title: Plurals: five patterns, one habit
body: German has no single plural ending like English *-s*. There are five patterns, and no rule can predict which pattern a word takes — so the plural gets learned along with the word too.

after: Dictionaries write it in shorthand: *der Stuhl, -"e* means the plural is *Stühle*; *die Tür, -en* means *Türen*. Once you're used to reading those marks, one dictionary line holds everything you need to learn.

The way of learning that saves the most time: learn **three things at once** in one breath — *der Stuhl, die Stühle*. Learning the word first, the gender later and the plural later still means learning the same word three times.

blocks.text: Learn the whole row, not just the middle column. A wrong article won't stop people understanding you, but it spreads everywhere once you reach the Akkusativ and Dativ.

⚠️ *Das Handy* is an English word that English speakers don't use — you'd say *cell phone* or *mobile*. German is full of words like this (*das Handy*, *der Beamer*, *das Public Viewing*); people call them *Scheinanglizismus*, "fake English".
English already has a rough version of this split: *no* or *not a* before nouns (*no time*, *not a book*), *not* everywhere else. German makes it strict.

blocks.text: Quick rule of thumb: if the noun could take *ein/eine* or stands with no article, use **kein**. If it already has *der/die/das*, *mein*, or is a person's name, use **nicht**.

items: *Kein Problem!* — No problem! (note: *kein*, because *Problem* is a noun)
